title: The best career advice came from a gardener
take: He doesn’t wear a watch: “now is the most important time. Just dedicate yourself to now.”

title: Why he wouldn’t start a company again
take: Asked on Acquired what he’d build at 30 today, he says “I wouldn’t do it.” NVIDIA was far harder than any founder expects.

title: Quitting at 30, with young kids, to found NVIDIA
take: He left LSI Logic in 1993. He explains how he made the call as a parent.

title: Innovation requires failure
take: “Unless you have a tolerance for failure, you will never experiment. If you don’t experiment you won’t innovate.”

title: “Passion isn’t enough, you’ve got to endure”
take: His career advice in one line, from a clip posted on X.

title: “I really discourage 1-on-1s”
take: He runs about 60 direct reports. He explains the reasoning to Stripe’s Patrick Collison.

title: His 5-step algorithm for running companies
take: Step one: “make your requirements less dumb.” Be most suspicious of requirements from smart people.

title: Smash your ego, internalize responsibility
take: At a startup, CEO or not, you do whatever the task takes and keep ego out of it.

title: His life philosophy
take: Why he cares about sustainable energy and making humans multi-planetary, traced back to a teenage search for meaning.

title: The teenage crisis that gave him a purpose
take: He found meaning in preserving and expanding consciousness and exploring the universe.

title: How Zip2 started
take: He dropped out of a Stanford PhD and wrote early maps, directions and yellow pages for the web. He didn’t plan to start a company.

title: Running Tesla and SpaceX in the same week
take: A 2013 clip on how he split his schedule between the two companies.

title: The five things he looks for in a founder
take: Starts with “I always figure it out” and “I never give up.”

title: Be relentlessly resourceful
take: The Paul Graham advice he says never got enough credit: keep finding new angles of attack.

title: “Most people don’t take enough risk”
take: People are wrong about what is risky, especially early in a career.

title: What he wishes he knew at YC in 2005
take: Conviction and resilience over a long period of time.

title: “No matter how great your idea is, no one cares”
take: His answer to founders who worry someone will steal an idea.

title: “One of the few arbitrage opportunities left is time”
take: His edge is committing to something for a very long time.

title: What he learned from Peter Thiel
take: On Thiel’s knack for short statements that stick, like “We wanted flying cars, instead we got 140 characters.”

title: “I’ve never met someone successful who had a great social life at 20”
take: His advice to young people in the age of AI: find what you’re uniquely good at and organize your life around it.

title: How to stay valuable when LLMs make general knowledge cheap
take: He argues general knowledge is now a commodity, so deep, specific skill is what gets rewarded.

title: Palantir doesn’t hire the all-A student
take: On why elite-school polish is not what the company is screening for.

title: What makes a Palantirian
take: How the founding team called their smartest friends and set out to change the world.

title: Why he has a bone to pick with Wall Street
take: A short interview clip on his dispute with the finance crowd.

title: “Why do we have a Department of Defense? We should have a Department of Offense”
take: On the L3Harris partnership and the company’s patriotic positioning.

title: How he planned to save Apple from bankruptcy
take: A CNBC interview three months after he returned in 1997, asked about the turnaround strategy.

title: “If you do the right things on the top line, the bottom line will follow”
take: A short CNBC clip on running a company for the product, not the numbers.

title: “A tremendous amount of craftsmanship between a great idea and a great product”
take: He also names the disease that hurt Apple after he left.

title: “One product, one focus”
take: The advice he gave Marc Benioff before Salesforce took off.

title: Walks off a 1998 interview
take: A CNBC classic: he reacts to a question about Apple and leaves.

title: The best advice Peter Thiel gave him
take: “In a world that’s changing so quickly, the biggest risk you can take is not taking any risk.”

title: “You can’t 80/20 everything”
take: Paul Graham asks if early Facebook would have worked without its details. His answer is about doing some work past 80 percent.

title: “There’s a difference between building good things and building awesome things”
take: The distinction he picked up from Palmer Luckey and the early Oculus team.

title: “If I can build Facebook, you can build a search engine”
take: A new hire recalls what Zuckerberg said a few weeks into the job in 2005.

title: The Steve Jobs advice he kept to himself
take: Offered $1 billion for Facebook, he says Jobs told him to visit a temple in India. A repost of his on-stage telling.

title: Why he got into biology
take: He and his sister lost their father to a disease that became curable a few years later, which drives his belief that AI can bring cures sooner.

title: “I’d rather they make fun of me”
take: On CBS, he explains why he keeps warning about AI risks despite the ridicule.

title: An age of miracles
take: He says cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease and mental illness could be relics of the past in under a decade.

title: Drive at 90, not 200
take: His pacing analogy for why Anthropic slows down on purpose.

title: His GPT-2 freakout in 2019
take: He recalls GPT-2 as the first real test of the scaling hypothesis.

title: Open source is a red herring
take: He argues that for AI, what matters is whether a model is good, not whether it is open.

title: “Missionaries build better products”
take: To Charlie Rose, using Sony’s postwar mission as the example.

title: He called customer service mid-meeting to prove a metric wrong
take: Metrics said customers waited under 60 seconds. He dialed in and found out.

title: What “disagree and commit” means
take: A principle he says “saves a lot of arguing.”

title: Too many ideas can destroy a company
take: The “releasing the work” idea: every idea released is a backlog of work in process.

title: Plan around what won’t change in 10 years
take: Build strategy on stable things, like customers wanting low prices and fast delivery.

title: “The hardest thing I’ve ever done”
take: Raising Amazon’s seed round: 20% of the company for $1 million from 22 angels, after about 60 meetings.

title: Don’t chase the hot new thing
take: Position yourself and wait for the wave to come to you.

title: The quiet genius behind TikTok’s global takeover
take: A third-party profile on YouTube. No short X clips of him turned up.

title: Gravitas: troubled times for TikTok’s founder
take: A news segment on the pressure around ByteDance, on YouTube.

title: From software engineer to global entrepreneur
take: A profile of his path, on YouTube.

title: Jensen Huang on his management style and succession
take: Unreleased footage from Emily Chang's recent interview for The Circuit, where Jensen Huang talks about his management style and who might succeed him.

title: Sam Altman at Semafor on AI marketing, safety and going public
take: Video clips from Sam Altman's Semafor Silicon Valley conversation, covering the need for better AI marketing, new safety risks, recursive self-improvement and how people see data centers. Asked about not going public, he points to journalist skepticism and bullish investors.

title: Bezos: an outside CEO is a last resort for Nvidia
take: Jeff Bezos says hiring an outside CEO would have a vanishingly small chance of success, and advises Nvidia's board to treat an outsider as a last resort.

title: Bezos on his AI startup Prometheus
take: Jeff Bezos describes Prometheus, which has raised $14.5B at a $41B valuation and is building an AI model to design and manufacture complex hardware, arguing you can't learn engineering by reading.

title: Amodei's IPO-day speech at the Nasdaq opening bell
take: Dario Amodei says powerful AI working with humans could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade, and that Anthropic will not bend to business or political pressure.

title: Karp on why AI will hurt the middle class
take: Alex Karp, in an interview titled as a warning that AI will hurt the middle class, argues you can't have billionaires becoming 100x wealthier.

title: Altman: it's hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen
take: Excerpt from Sam Altman's Semafor conversation in Menlo Park, titled as him crediting Jensen Huang's role in the AI revolution.

title: The Benjamin Franklin exercise for choosing who to be
take: To business students: imagine you could own 10% of one classmate’s lifetime earnings. Who would you pick? Probably not the one with the highest grades.

title: The best management advice he ever got
take: He credits his friend and mentor Tom Murphy, the broadcasting executive, as the best manager he knew.

title: “You can always tell someone to go to hell tomorrow”
take: Tom Murphy’s advice on waiting a day before reacting in anger.

title: One zero wipes out the whole chain
take: Multiply any string of strong returns by zero and the answer is zero, so avoid the one mistake that ends the game.

title: “Be selective about your friends”
take: A line from his CNBC interview: be selective about your friends and hope they aren’t too selective about theirs.

title: Two types of companies in the age of AI
take: Those great at AI and those that have gone out of business. He also splits people into those who use AI to learn and those who use it to avoid learning.

title: How to start a business without raising money
take: He says at least 90 to 95 percent of small businesses can start with sweat equity and no outside capital.

title: “Sales cures all”
take: His advice to every first-time founder.

title: No such thing as work-life balance if you want to win
take: He describes going seven years without a vacation when he was building his first business.

title: Stop worrying about your failures
take: Speaking at the Global Entrepreneurship Congress: get up, get over it, and move on.

title: Steve Jobs taught him “everything’s a remix”
take: On a TechCrunch podcast, he explains how that idea shaped how he builds and invests.

title: “If you had a year left to live, would you still take this job?”
take: The question he asked the first 300 Airbnb hires, to find people who cared about the mission.

title: 100 customers who love you beat a million who like you
take: Paul Graham’s advice that helped Airbnb find product/market fit.

title: How to interview and reference-check new hires
take: Start with the results and work backwards to the people, not with resumes and brands. He credits Steve Jobs for the idea.

title: Design the perfect experience for one person
take: It is easier to start with one person than to design for a million.

title: The one rule Airbnb’s cofounders had
take: Winning an argument was never more important than preserving the relationship.

title: Renting rooms to strangers: “the worst idea ever”
take: He shares Airbnb’s origin story, including how investors saw the idea at first.

title: “Working with people you’re close to is underrated”
take: He started Stripe with his brother John and the Arc Institute with his wife Silvana.

title: Advice for your 20s: work at a place with high standards
take: He points to the book Apprentice to Genius, about three generations of scientists who mentored each other.

title: Be okay waiting a very long time to hire
take: It took Stripe six months to hire its first two people. Great people already have good options, so you have to be persistent.

title: What startups get wrong before product/market fit
take: The main mistake is speed of iteration.

title: You won’t succeed doing what everyone else is doing
take: His standard advice: as an entrepreneur, find the errors in conventional wisdom.

title: What made Steve Jobs great
take: He tells the peacock story: how he met his future best friend of about 25 years.

title: Leadership and confidence
take: “You cannot lead if you’re filled with uncertainty,” illustrated with a story about two officers leading Marines up a hill.

title: The dinner with Jensen Huang and Elon Musk
take: He jokes that it was Oracle, himself and Elon begging Jensen for GPUs.

title: “Pick hard problems to solve and be ambitious with them”
take: In his official Nobel Prize interview, on why timing matters.

title: AI models going rogue are “warning shots”
take: From his WSJ Magazine Job Interview: security and regulation should be dealt with before the systems get more powerful.

title: The first thing he wanted to apply AI to was human health
take: On Fortune’s Titans and Disruptors of Industry, about why he founded Isomorphic Labs.

title: On why schools should change because of AGI
take: He argues schools are still teaching skills AI will be better at. Critics dispute the point.
